meta.question: Under what input distributions and sizes does a hybrid merge/insertion sorting strategy outperform predefined baselines without violating correctness, and what insertion cutoff is optimal per regime?

plan.question: Under what input distributions and sizes does a hybrid merge/insertion sorting strategy outperform predefined baselines without violating correctness, and what insertion cutoff is optimal per regime?

src_4c8df7ee3c.title: Standard algorithm-analysis results (seeded; Phase 2 replaces with live source acquisition)

clm_bbc4b6ecee.text: Any comparison sort requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

clm_2a22e5624c.text: Insertion sort runs in O(n + inversions); it is linear on nearly-sorted input.

clm_6241b012d7.text: Quicksort's worst case is O(n^2), but median-of-three pivoting avoids it on sorted/reversed inputs.

clm_7060fe4c45.text: Hybrid insertion-cutoff optima at n=4096 (7 trials, CPython 3.12.3 on Linux/x86_64): random=16 (indistinguishable from [8, 32]), nearly_sorted=64 (indistinguishable from [32]), reversed=8 (indistinguishable from [16]), few_unique=16 (indistinguishable from [8, 32])

hyp_dbe5f386a7.statement: Insertion sort is the fastest candidate on nearly-sorted input, and the slowest on random input, at the tested sizes.
hyp_dbe5f386a7.rationale: Adaptive O(n + inversions) behavior dominates on low-inversion input; O(n^2) dominates on random input.

predictions.detail: fastest_on on 'nearly_sorted' is insertion_sort (0.5 ms, margin 704% over shell_sort, separation 3.45 ms > required 0.07 ms) [n=4096, 7 trials]
slowest_on on 'random' is insertion_sort (375.7 ms, margin 1802% over shell_sort, separation 355.94 ms > required 9.65 ms) [n=4096, 7 trials]

hyp_dbe5f386a7.scope: holds at n<=2x tested sizes on its original regime(s); does NOT extend to ['organ_pipe', 'sawtooth']

hyp_fa035de7df.statement: Merge sort is the fastest pure-Python candidate on random input.
hyp_fa035de7df.rationale: Guaranteed n log n with sequential memory access; no pathological cases.

predictions.detail: fastest_on on 'random' is quick_sort, not merge_sort (71% apart, decisive) [n=4096, 7 trials]

hyp_cae1c60f85.statement: Quick sort (median-of-three, Hoare) stays within 25% of the best candidate on random input and does not collapse on reversed input.
hyp_cae1c60f85.rationale: MO3 pivoting neutralizes ordered-input pathologies; constant factors are low.

predictions.text: quick_sort within 25% of best on random
predictions.detail: quick_sort is 0% off best on 'random' (limit 25%, uncertainty ±24%) [n=4096, 7 trials]

predictions.text: quick_sort within 200% of best on reversed
predictions.detail: quick_sort is 0% off best on 'reversed' (limit 200%, uncertainty ±4%) [n=4096, 7 trials]

hyp_ad33a3dcb5.statement: Heap sort is the most consistent candidate (lowest relative timing variance across regimes) but is never the fastest in any regime.
hyp_ad33a3dcb5.rationale: Input-oblivious n log n behavior; poor cache locality keeps constants high.

predictions.text: heap_sort has lowest mean relative stdev
predictions.detail: lowest mean relative stdev: merge_sort (0.050); next is quick_sort (0.063) [n=4096, 7 trials]

predictions.text: heap_sort is never fastest in any regime

hyp_40df9834c7.statement: Shell sort beats insertion sort on random input but not on nearly-sorted input at the tested sizes.
hyp_40df9834c7.rationale: [mock proposal prop_92794c6d1c] Gap sequences reduce long-distance disorder faster than adjacent swaps; on nearly-sorted data insertion sort's adaptivity should dominate.

predictions.text: Shell sort beats insertion sort on random input but not on nearly-sorted input at the tested sizes.
predictions.detail: shell_sort vs insertion_sort on 'random': +739% (needs >= 0.0%, decisive: gap 19.45 ms > required 1.39 ms) [n=1024, 7 trials]

hyp_f1699d47b3.statement: Heap sort beats shell sort on reversed input at the tested sizes.
hyp_f1699d47b3.rationale: [mock proposal prop_b8a25c4aab] Reversed input is adversarial for gap/insertion strategies while heap construction cost is input-independent.

predictions.text: Heap sort beats shell sort on reversed input at the tested sizes.
predictions.detail: heap_sort is decisively SLOWER than shell_sort on 'reversed' (-30%) [n=4096, 7 trials]

hyp_38e7e1fe16.statement: A hybrid algorithm (merge sort with insertion-sort cutoff <= 32) beats plain merge sort on random AND nearly-sorted input at the tested sizes.
hyp_38e7e1fe16.rationale: Round-1 evidence: 'insertion_sort' won nearly_sorted and 'quick_sort' won random. Combining merge structure with insertion's strength on short/ordered runs should reduce recursion overhead without losing n log n guarantees. Derived from experiment exp_c512323528.

predictions.text: hybrid_sort beats merge_sort on random by >= 5%
predictions.detail: hybrid_sort vs merge_sort on 'random': +53% (needs >= 5%, decisive: gap 3.24 ms > required 0.62 ms) [n=4096, 7 trials]
hybrid_sort vs merge_sort on 'nearly_sorted': +182% (needs >= 0%, decisive: gap 4.41 ms > required 0.93 ms) [n=4096, 7 trials]

hyp_bf17e1f36c.statement: The hybrid's optimal insertion cutoff on random input lies in [16, 64], and the optimal cutoff on nearly-sorted input is >= the optimum on random input.
hyp_bf17e1f36c.rationale: Python call overhead favors moderate cutoffs; insertion sort's adaptivity should tolerate larger segments on nearly-sorted data. Pre-registered before any sweep ran.

predictions.detail: best cutoff on random = 16 (inside [16,64]) but cutoffs [8] are statistically indistinguishable from it at 7 trials — the optimum is not resolvable to that interval

predictions.text: optimal cutoff on nearly_sorted >= optimal on random
predictions.detail: optimum nearly_sorted=64 vs random=16, but the optima are not uniquely identified (indistinguishable sets: nearly_sorted=[32, 64], random=[8, 16, 32])

assumptions: Wall-clock time on a single machine/interpreter is an acceptable proxy for algorithmic cost at these sizes.
Pure-Python implementations are compared against each other only; C-accelerated builtins are out of scope for fairness.
The four tested input regimes are representative of the distributions of interest.
All timings come from a single machine and interpreter; absolute numbers will not transfer, only rankings might.
Conclusions hold only for the tested input regimes and sizes; extrapolation beyond them is speculation, not inference.
